1.pericope_label: The word of the Lord came again unto me, saying, Now, thou son of man, take up a lamentation for Tyrus; And say unto Tyrus, O thou that art situate at the entry of the sea, which art a merchant of the people for many isles, Thus saith the Lord God; O Tyrus, thou hast said, I am of perfect beauty. Thy borders are in the midst of the seas, thy builders have perfected thy beauty.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch render the opening verses plainly, the city dwelling at the approaches of the sea, merchant of the nations to many islands, its territory in the heart of the seas and its beauty perfected by its builders; Ellicott presses the wording of the site, since the term rendered entry is plural and means approaches or harbours, of which Tyre had two, both excellent, one facing south and the other north with an outer roadstead formed by a ledge off the island's north-west point, the first now wholly and the second nearly choked with sand and ruins.

Gill describes the elegy as a funeral song of the kind the mourning women sang, saying all that could be said in praise of the dead, and draws from it that even wicked men are to be pitied in calamity; he places the city at the eastern end of the great sea, half a mile off the mainland and well placed for shipping, and notes that its borders stood in the midst of the seas until a Macedonian siege turned the island into a peninsula.

Clarke calls the chapter the second part of the prophecy against Tyre, conducted in the manner of the old laments in which hired mourners first recited whatever was great in the dead and then wept for the fall, so that the riches fill most of the chapter, the ruin is dispatched in a single allegorical verse of astonishing brevity, and the maritime world is left alarmed for itself; he calls the site a small island or rather a rock, notes that a second Tyre stood on the shore with the two reckoned one city, identifies the allegory of the ship at once, and sets beside it a Latin ode in which a commonwealth is drawn the same way, a vessel with stripped decks, wounded mast, groaning yards and torn sails, warned that a painted stern is no comfort in a storm; Wesley gives the distance from the continent as four furlongs, the city lying as it were in the very door of the sea, and repeats Henry's principle about mourning for other nations almost word for word.

Henry explains why a lament is called for while the city still stands at the height of its prosperity, since that prosperity is the snare and feeds a pride that will make the fall worse, and those who live at ease are to be lamented if they are not preparing for trouble; he states that we ought to mourn for the miseries of other nations as well as our own out of an affection for mankind in general, even where a people have brought the trouble on themselves, adding that bewailing their calamities is part of the honour owed to all men; on the boast of perfect beauty he sets against it the older title given to Zion, called the perfection of beauty because it had the beauty of holiness, and concludes that nobody should count himself beautified further than he is sanctified or claim perfect beauty on this side of heaven; and he notes that the encomium is conventional in elegies, while observing what the prophet cannot praise, since nothing is said of Tyre's religion, her piety or her charity.

debates.question: Why compose a lament for a city still at its height?

positions.position: Because prosperity is the snare that feeds the pride which makes the fall worse, and those at ease are to be lamented if they are not preparing for trouble.
Because the form requires it: the old funeral songs first recited whatever was great in the dead and only then wept for the fall.
Because even wicked men are to be pitied when in distress and calamity.

debates.question: What does the phrase about the entry of the sea describe?

positions.position: A plural term meaning approaches or harbours: Tyre had two excellent ones, now choked with sand and ruins.
The island's position half a mile off the mainland, well placed for shipping and a harbour.
A rock at a short distance from the shore, with a second Tyre on the mainland, the two reckoned one city.

outliers.claim: Sets a Latin ode alongside the chapter, in which a commonwealth is drawn as a storm-beaten ship with stripped decks and torn sails, offering it as a parallel to the prophet's allegory.
Reads the silence of the encomium: the prophet praises everything praiseworthy in Tyre and so says nothing at all of her religion, her piety, or her charity to neighbours in distress.

themes: The word of the Lord came again unto me, saying,

5.pericope_label: They have made all thy ship boards of fir trees of Senir: they have taken cedars from Lebanon to make masts for thee. Of the oaks of Bashan have they made thine oars; the company of the Ashurites have made thy benches of ivory, brought out of the isles of Chittim. Fine linen with broidered work from Egypt was that which thou spreadest forth to be thy sail; blue and purple from the isles of Elishah was that which covered thee. The inhabitants of Zidon and Arvad were thy mariners: thy wise men, O Tyrus, that were in thee, were thy pilots. The ancients of Gebal and the wise men thereof were in thee thy calkers: all the ships of the sea with their mariners were in thee to occupy thy merchandise. They of Persia and of Lud and of Phut were in thine army, thy men of war: they hanged the shield and helmet in thee; they set forth thy comeliness. The men of Arvad with thine army were upon thy walls round about, and the Gammadims were in thy towers: they hanged their shields upon thy walls round about; they have made thy beauty perfect.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch describe the hired troops from abroad protecting the colonies while Phoenicians manned the walls, identify two of the three mercenary peoples as African rather than Asiatic, and find the mention of Persia the surprising item in the list; Ellicott confirms that the word for planking is dual, referring to the two sides of the hull, explains the unfamiliar mountain name by supposing the prophet wanted a foreign one whose alternative had fallen out of use, admits that the Scripture names of trees are not always well identified and that the timber here may be spruce or cypress, sets out the two doubtful words in the verse about benches so that the clause reads literally that they made thy something of tooth, daughter of something, argues that the first must mean planking and probably decking since it is singular, joins the two Hebrew words presently written apart to yield in box-wood, defends linen sails as normal in the state ships of antiquity with the embroidery serving instead of a pennon, places the source of the purple on the coasts of Asia Minor, has the Phoenician towns furnish the oarsmen while Tyre supplied the captains and pilots, notes that the figure of the ship is dropped when the soldiers are described so that the military strength can be stated plainly, and denies that any people of the last name is known, thinking it unlikely that watch-towers would be manned by foreigners and preferring to translate the word brave men.

Gill takes the dual form of the word for planking as the two sides of the hull, notes that the oaks supplied only the oars though the country was famous for oaks and one might have expected hulls, supposes the ships were galleys, and reports what travellers of his own day found on the island that sent the rowers, a magnificent prospect from the mainland that resolves on arrival into one weak castle with a few small guns.

Clarke identifies the mountain with the one the Sidonians called Sirion, reports that some render the oar-wood alder and others pine, takes the disputed term for boxwood, thinks the flag rather than the sail is meant by the linen, places the source of the purple in the Peloponnese, explains what caulking is as hemp and pitch driven into the seams, remarks drily that skilful and desperate men will go anywhere after their price, and on the last name lists a Phoenician people, guardian images and simply strong men while dismissing the old rendering that made them pygmies a cubit high; Wesley has box shipped from the Aegean and inlaid with ivory by Tyrian craftsmen, places the purple in Aeolis among people skilled at dyeing wool and calls the ship's covering what a boatman would call a tilt, says the rich Tyrians would not employ their own in servile work and hired strangers while keeping their learned men for navigation, which was their great study, and guesses that the last name belongs to a town called Gammade.

debates.question: What did they make of ivory and box, and how should the clause be read?

positions.position: Two words are doubtful; the first must be planking and probably decking, since it is singular where benches would be plural, and joining the two Hebrew words presently written apart yields in box-wood.
Benches of boxwood inlaid with ivory, the wood coming from islands variously identified.
Box shipped from the Aegean, sawn into boards for benches and inlaid with ivory by Tyrian craftsmen.

debates.question: Who or what were the Gammadims in the towers?

positions.position: Not a people at all: no such nation is known, watch-towers would hardly be manned by foreigners, and the word should be translated brave men.
Possibly a Phoenician people, possibly guardian images, possibly simply strong men acting as guards; not pygmies a cubit high, as an old rendering had it.
Probably men of Gammade, a town of Phoenicia.

outliers.claim: Concedes that the Scripture names of trees are not always well identified, so that the timber called fir here may be either spruce or cypress, the latter prized in shipbuilding for lightness and freedom from worm.
Explains the mercenary lists in one dry sentence, that skilful and desperate men will go anywhere after their price.

12.pericope_label: Tarshish was thy merchant by reason of the multitude of all kind of riches; with silver, iron, tin, and lead, they traded in thy fairs. Javan, Tubal, and Meshech, they were thy merchants: they traded the persons of men and vessels of brass in thy market. They of the house of Togarmah traded in thy fairs with horses and horsemen and mules. The men of Dedan were thy merchants; many isles were the merchandise of thine hand: they brought thee for a present horns of ivory and ebony. Syria was thy merchant by reason of the multitude of the wares of thy making: they occupied in thy fairs with emeralds, purple, and broidered work, and fine linen, and coral, and agate. Judah, and the land of Israel, they were thy merchants: they traded in thy market wheat of Minnith, and Pannag, and honey, and oil, and balm. Damascus was thy merchant in the multitude of the wares of thy making, for the multitude of all riches; in the wine of Helbon, and white wool. Dan also and Javan going to and fro occupied in thy fairs: bright iron, cassia, and calamus, were in thy market. Dedan was thy merchant in precious clothes for chariots. Arabia, and all the princes of Kedar, they occupied with thee in lambs, and rams, and goats: in these were they thy merchants. The merchants of Sheba and Raamah, they were thy merchants: they occupied in thy fairs with chief of all spices, and with all precious stones, and gold. Haran, and Canneh, and Eden, the merchants of Sheba, Asshur, and Chilmad, were thy merchants. These were thy merchants in all sorts of things, in blue clothes, and broidered work, and in chests of rich apparel, bound with cords, and made of cedar, among thy merchandise. The ships of Tarshish did sing of thee in thy market: and thou wast replenished, and made very glorious in the midst of the seas.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch refuse both to emend the disputed name in the middle of the catalogue and to render it as the tribe of Dan, holding it decisive that throughout the whole enumeration not a single land or people is introduced with that copula, and take it instead for a tribe and tract not named elsewhere, conjectured to be Aden, with the following name standing not for Greece but for an Arabian district; Ellicott explains that the term rendered fairs occurs only in this chapter and should be rendered wares throughout, its idea being something left with one party in place of something given in exchange, since ancient commerce was chiefly barter, reads the section as a survey of the nations not already named with the prophet varying his synonyms to avoid monotony, locates Tarshish in Spain and its metals, identifies the slave-dealing tribes as the Tibareni and Moschi between the Black and Caspian seas whose mountains still hold copper, gives the same grammatical argument about the conjunction, separates a Hamite Dedan on the Persian Gulf from a Semitic one named later, glosses horns of ivory as horns of teeth and notes that the word for ebony occurs only here, places the wheat country in Ammon while confessing the next word unknown and possibly not a place name but a sweet confection, corrects chests of rich apparel to treasures of twisted yarn and made of cedar to strong, and explains that ships of Tarshish means simply vessels of the largest class while the word taken for singers is uncertain between bulwarks and caravans.
Gill records the reading that takes the name of the first trading nation simply for the sea rather than for a place.

Clarke observes that the places and their imports are entered as regularly as they would be in a European custom-house, canvasses the Carthaginians, a port near the western straits and a town in Cilicia for the first name, notes the metals it was famous for and that all of them might have come from Britain, will not let the slave entry pass without remarking that the bodies and souls of men were bought and sold then as in his own degenerate age, keeps both of the disputed names Greek and takes the phrase rendered going to and fro for importing and exporting while allowing that it may be a proper name, and suspects that the clause about the wheat country names goods rather than towns; Wesley notes only that the northern peoples brought men to sell for slaves, and calls the unidentified name beside the wheat country an obscure place now forgotten.

debates.question: How should the disputed name in the middle of the catalogue be read?

positions.position: Not as the tribe of Dan: the supposed conjunction is part of a name, an Arabian place some identify with Aden, and the name beside it is an Arabian district rather than Greece.
The same conclusion on the same ground, that nowhere else in the enumeration is a land or people introduced with that copula.
Both names are Greek, and the phrase rendered going to and fro means importing and exporting, though it may be a proper name.
Tartessus in Spain, famous for the metals named, silver above all.
Perhaps the Carthaginians, perhaps a port near the western straits, perhaps a town in Cilicia; the metals might all have come from Britain.
Some take the name simply for the sea.

outliers.claim: Breaks off the geography to note that these peoples trafficked in slaves, and that the bodies and souls of men were bought and sold in those days as in his own degenerate age.
Admits that one name in the list is simply unknown, and may not be a place name at all but the name of a sweet confection such as grape syrup.

26.pericope_label: Thy rowers have brought thee into great waters: the east wind hath broken thee in the midst of the seas. Thy riches, and thy fairs, thy merchandise, thy mariners, and thy pilots, thy calkers, and the occupiers of thy merchandise, and all thy men of war, that are in thee, and in all thy company which is in the midst of thee, shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin. The suburbs shall shake at the sound of the cry of thy pilots. And all that handle the oar, the mariners, and all the pilots of the sea, shall come down from their ships, they shall stand upon the land; And shall cause their voice to be heard against thee, and shall cry bitterly, and shall cast up dust upon their heads, they shall wallow themselves in the ashes: And they shall make themselves utterly bald for thee, and gird them with sackcloth, and they shall weep for thee with bitterness of heart and bitter wailing. And in their wailing they shall take up a lamentation for thee, and lament over thee, saying, What city is like Tyrus, like the destroyed in the midst of the sea? When thy wares went forth out of the seas, thou filledst many people; thou didst enrich the kings of the earth with the multitude of thy riches and of thy merchandise. In the time when thou shalt be broken by the seas in the depths of the waters thy merchandise and all thy company in the midst of thee shall fall. All the inhabitants of the isles shall be astonished at thee, and their kings shall be sore afraid, they shall be troubled in their countenance. The merchants among the people shall hiss at thee; thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt be any more.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch render the roll of what sinks — the riches and sales, the bartering wares, seamen and sailors, the repairers of leaks and the treaders in wares, the fighting men and all the multitude — and observe that the ruin causes such consternation that sailors abandon their own ships as no longer safe, the prophet heaping up every customary act of grief at once, dust, ashes, the shaved head, sackcloth, bitter weeping and a dirge; Ellicott notes that oars were the main means of moving a ship before sailing was well understood and that the east wind of that sea is genuinely dangerous, presses the small word that should be read with rather than in so that every class making up the city's strength goes down with the ship, explains that the word rendered suburbs means the open ground about a place and must here mean Tyre's surroundings generally since she had no land around her, makes the colonies and dependencies the smaller craft that escape to shore, corrects against thee to over thee since the trading nations were not hostile, and denies that the closing verb means derision or terror at all, giving it the sense of calling for, so that those who traded with her will call and she will not answer.

Gill makes the rowers the rulers and inhabitants and the great waters the straits they brought on themselves by provoking Babylon, notes that what was years in gathering was lost in a day, has the cry carrying to the mainland and the towns belonging to the city, and keeps the plainer sense of scorn for the closing verb, recalling that Tyre had done the same over Jerusalem in hope of inheriting her trade.

Clarke has the trading vessels of every nation towing the city into deep water, which is to say into affluence, before the storm dashes her to pieces, puts the wreck flatly, that laden with valuables and manned as well as a ship could be she struck and all of it went to the bottom, and then abandons commentary to testify, having heard the cry raised when a ship is driven on rocks with the helm useless, saying nothing more dismal can be imagined and that the shout when all is lost is worse than the cry of fire at midnight, and describing a scene he witnessed himself among the wretched; on the closing verb he takes the hissing for a shriek, the sound spectators make as a vessel goes under; Wesley makes the rowers the governors and counsellors, reads the east wind as the king of Babylon with his army and the past tense as certainty, and notes the sting in the place of the breaking, where the city thought herself impregnable.

Henry draws the moral without softening it, that the most magnificent states have their day to come down and begin to decline at the zenith, that this ruin was sudden with the sun going down at noon, and that the wealth which made the city great made the fall more grievous; the ship was split by the indiscretion of her own steersmen, who involved her in a war by mismanagement and then, holding out obstinately, enraged the enemy into destroying the state altogether, so that it goes ill with a people when those at the stern do not steer them into safety.

debates.question: What does the closing hissing of the merchants mean?

positions.position: Not derision or terror but calling for: those who traded with her will call, and she will not answer, being a sudden end and not for ever.
A shriek, the sound spectators on the shore make as a vessel goes under.
Plain scorn, the merchants hissing as Tyre had hissed over Jerusalem in hope of inheriting her trade.

debates.question: Who brought the city to ruin?

positions.position: Her own steersmen, who mismanaged her into the war and then enraged the enemy by holding out obstinately.
Her rulers and inhabitants, who provoked Babylon by some unadvised step.
The east wind, that is the king of Babylon with his army, breaking her where she thought herself impregnable.

outliers.claim: Stops commenting to testify from his own experience of shipwreck on a lee shore, saying the cry when all is lost is worse than the cry of fire at midnight and that he was one of the wretched who made it.
Notices that the mourners abandon their own ships as though no longer safe in them, and that the prophet heaps every customary rite of grief into one passage.
